newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - French insurer Axa first-half profit leaps.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - French insurer Axa first-half profit leaps.

text.p: French insurance giant Axa SA reported on Wednesday that first-half profits rocketed 52 percent, powered by strong performances by its non-life activities and U.S. financial services.
Confirming its reputation as the country's most profitable insurer, Axa said net consolidated profit climbed to 1.98 billion francs ($388 million) from 1.30 billion francs a year earlier.
Group turnover, at 87.5 billion francs, rose 21.2 percent while earnings per share climbed 33.1 percent to 10.57 francs.

The showing by Axa, the lone French insurer whose balance sheet has not been hammered by exposure to a long-running property slump, beat most analysts' expectations and drove the shares up nearly four percent to 297 francs.
"It's a very good set of numbers," an analyst said. "Axa is the best (French) insurance stock in the market," a trader said.
Chairman Claude Bebear told an analysts' meeting that he expected a good second half but that it would "be a bit optimistic" to expect it to match the first half.

Axa, which has grown from a sleepy mutual company in the 1980s into a globl player that now earns less than a third of its profit in France, said it was aiming for a 15 percent return on equity after the year 2000, up from 10.9 percent currently.
It forecast annual earnings per share growth above 15 percent to the year 2000.
Seeking to defuse market rumours, Bebear said no talks were under way with rival UAP, whose shares were boosted recently by speculation Axa was eyeing it as a takeover target.

Bebear, who recently declared Axa had a 30 billion franc war chest, also said there were no talks of any importance under way with other groups. "At the moment we are in no discussions of any significance with anyone," he said.

Axa's earnings were powered by a near doubling of non-life insurance profits to 610 million francs from 320 million. Financial services, whose profits leapt to 618 million francs from 397 million francs, were another driving factor.

Especially important was the contribution from investment bank Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette of the United States which sharply increased its profit contribution to 343 million francs, up from 198 million francs.
Australian life insurer National Mutual, acquired by Axa last year to serve as a springboard for entry into Asia, contributed 13 million francs.

Life insurance, however, kicked in with 504 million francs versus 555 million francs last time. This was due partly to a lower contribution from U.S. life that reflected a 72 million franc exceptional charge related to changes in accounting principles.

The poorer life performance also reflected a 58 million franc negative contribution from German activities, due partly to accounting changes, as well as start-up costs related to its Japanese life insurance company.
The Japanese operations lost 84 million francs in the first half. ($1=5.101 French Franc)
